name: Bustle and crinoline

lead: The crinoline and the bustle were supports worn under women's skirts in the nineteenth century. The crinoline, a steel-hooped cage from the 1850s, pushed skirts out in a wide dome; the bustle, from the 1870s, shifted fullness to the back.
Both changed the proportions of the body: a wide or rear-projecting skirt makes the waist look smaller and emphasizes the hips. They survive in bridal wear, couture and costume.

paras: They were worn as underlayers beneath the dress, usually with a corset; crinolines were hoops, bustles were pads or wire frames at the back below the waist. Today petticoat versions are worn for formal, bridal and period looks.

Historically, crinolines were highly flammable and snagged on objects; Florence Nightingale estimated at least 630 women died from clothing fires in 1863-1864. They also made moving through doors and sitting difficult.

angle.text: The garments change the outline directly. Contrast between a corseted waist and the extended skirt creates the hourglass look fashion of the period prized.

lead: The crinoline and the bustle are skirt supports that shaped women's silhouettes in the mid-to-late nineteenth century. By holding fabric out from the body, they made the waist appear smaller and the hips or rear fuller [1][2].

The cage crinoline arrived in the 1850s; a French patent was filed on 24 April 1856 and a British one that July [1]. Skirts could reach about six yards in circumference [1]. From about 1866 fashion moved to a flatter front with fullness behind, via the crinolette and then the bustle, which dominated the 1870s and 1880s and peaked around 1885 before fading by about 1905 [2][3].
No clinical studies exist on these garments; they are documented in fashion history.

paras: Crinoline began as the name of a stiff horsehair fabric, then of petticoats made from it, then of hooped cages; steel was the most common hoop material, while whalebone, cane, gutta-percha and inflatable rubber were tried [1]. The bustle was a padded or framed undergarment worn just below the waist to hold fabric at the back [2][3]. Earlier forms include the farthingale, panniers and the bum roll [1][2].

After the 1856 cage crinoline, skirts flattened at front and sides by the mid-1860s, and the bustle replaced the crinoline in the early 1870s [1][2]. A larger bustle appeared in 1881, peaked around 1885 and faded by 1889, with the longer corset shaping the body itself by about 1905 [2].
Crinolines returned in revived forms: the 1947 New Look, 1950s net petticoats and Vivienne Westwood's 1980s 'mini-crini' [1].

Crinolines were flammable and snagged on objects or caught the wind [1]. Nightingale estimated at least 630 women died in clothing fires in 1863-1864, and a December 1863 church fire in Santiago, Chile, killed thousands, with the dresses cited as a factor [1].
